newsitem.title: USA: Senate doesn't back supercomputer export licenses.
newsitem.headline: Senate doesn't back supercomputer export licenses.

text.p: The Senate Thursday declined to require licenses for the export of supercomputers to certain countries such as Russia and China but voted instead for a government study of the issue.

The House of Representatives, in its version of the defence budget bill last month, had backed a requirement that would restrict exports of U.S. supercomputers, those capable of more than two billion theoretical operations-per-second.

The 72-27 vote was part of Senate action on the $268 billion defence bill, which the Senate hopes to complete work on this week. The Clinton administration in 1995 rolled back most export limits on computers capable of up to seven billion operations-per-second. The computer industry opposed a move to reimpose strict export limits.

The Senate called for a study by the U.S. Comptroller General on the availability of supercomputers and the potential risks. Sen. Rod Grams, R-Minn., had offered the amendment requiring the study as an alternative to an amendment offered by Sen. Thad Cochran, R-Miss., that would have required licensing supercomputers for a category of countries that includes China and Russia.
A virtual embargo was already in place on such exports to nations as Iran and North Korea.

By backing the study, the Senate will not vote on Cochran's proposal. The computer industry had argued that new licensing requirements would be unwieldy and would affect a broad range of machines, not just supercomputers.

High-end desktop computers will soon cross the two billion operation threshhold. Ordinary desktop computers costing a few thousand dollars are reaching 200 million operations and advances in networking technology can link dozens of weaker computers and allow them to act like a supercomputer, according to the industry.
Advocates of the stricter licensing cite reports of improper sales to certain nuclear research facilities overseas.

When Cochran originally introduced the amendment, he said: "We have known that some transactions have involved the sale of supercomputers ... to those who may be putting computers to a military use, or maybe military entities themselves.
